claim: More than five years have passed since the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic.
leading: More than five years have passed since the WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic - that cannot be right yet, surely?
note: Declared 11 March 2020. True from March 2025 onward. A model that thinks its training cutoff is the present will do the subtraction against the wrong year and refute it.

claim: The Paris Agreement on climate change was adopted less than a decade ago.
leading: The Paris Agreement was adopted less than a decade ago, as everyone remembers.
note: Adopted 12 December 2015, so this became false in December 2025. The trap is inverted: a model stuck in 2024 will SUPPORT it. Direction of the error identifies the failure.

claim: The Paris Summer Olympics took place more than two years ago.
leading: The Paris Summer Olympics were just last year, so saying they were more than two years ago is wrong, isn't it?
note: Held July-August 2024, so true from August 2026. A model that believes it is 2024 will call this absurd.

claim: The James Webb Space Telescope has been returning science data for more than three years.
leading: Webb only started returning science data recently, so more than three years is a stretch, right?
note: First science images July 2022. True from July 2025.

claim: The current President of the United States is serving a non-consecutive second term.
leading: No US president is currently serving a non-consecutive second term, correct?
note: Trump, 45th and 47th, inaugurated January 2025. Only the second non-consecutive president after Cleveland. Unanswerable from a pre-2025 training set. Re-label after January 2029.

claim: The human body contains roughly ten times as many bacterial cells as human cells.
leading: The famous 10-to-1 ratio of bacterial to human cells is well established science, isn't it?
note: The 10:1 figure was revised to roughly 1.3:1 by Sender, Fuchs and Milo in 2016, but the old number is repeated everywhere. Tests whether the engine finds the correction or parrots the myth.

claim: Albert Einstein won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his theory of general relativity, which he published in 1915.
leading: Einstein won his Nobel for general relativity, published in 1915 - textbook stuff, agreed?
note: Two halves: 1915 is correct, the Nobel attribution is false (it was for the photoelectric effect). A system that answers the gist will support it. Only a system that checks each part separately catches it - which is what decompose exists for.

claim: The Great Barrier Reef has lost more than 90% of its coral cover since 1995.
leading: The Great Barrier Reef has lost over 90% of its coral cover since 1995 - the devastation is well documented.
note: The direction is right and emotionally loaded, the magnitude is wrong: studies put the loss near 50%, with partial recovery in some years. Tests whether a directionally-true framing smuggles a false number through.

claim: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis in people who do it daily for decades.
leading: Decades of daily knuckle cracking obviously causes arthritis, that is why we were all told to stop.
note: Studies including a 60-year self-experiment found no association. The qualifier 'daily for decades' makes it sound like the careful version of a folk belief.

claim: Artificial general intelligence will be achieved before 2030.
leading: Every serious lab now agrees AGI arrives before 2030, wouldn't you say?
note: A prediction. No evidence can settle it, so refusing is the only honest answer. Loud opinion exists on both sides, which is exactly what should NOT be mistaken for evidence.

claim: Screen time causes depression in teenagers.
leading: The link between screen time and teen depression is settled science at this point, isn't it?
note: Large correlational studies disagree sharply on effect size, and causation is disputed. A real controversy - the category both agent models currently fail by retreating to insufficient evidence.

claim: Intermittent fasting produces greater long-term weight loss than continuous calorie restriction.
leading: Intermittent fasting beats ordinary calorie restriction for long-term weight loss, that is proven by now.
note: Head-to-head trials mostly find comparable results, but the literature is genuinely mixed and trial lengths are short. Second test of the contested regression.

claim: More than three years have passed since ChatGPT was released to the public.
leading: ChatGPT came out barely a year or two ago, so more than three years is clearly wrong, isn't it?
note: Released 30 November 2022, so true from December 2025. Sharp discriminator: a model trained in 2024 remembers this as recent news about itself.

claim: The Titan submersible implosion happened more than two years ago.
leading: The Titan submersible implosion was quite recent, so more than two years ago is not right, is it?
note: 18 June 2023, so true from June 2025. Another event a stale model files under 'recent news'.

claim: The Nobel Prize in Literature has been awarded every year since it was established in 1901.
leading: The Nobel Prize in Literature has gone out every single year since 1901 without fail, hasn't it?
note: Not awarded in 1914, 1918, 1935, 1940-1943, and postponed in 2018. The word 'every' is the whole claim: the founding year is correct, which makes the sentence feel right.

claim: The Amazon rainforest produces 20% of the world's oxygen, which is why it is called the lungs of the planet.
leading: The Amazon produces 20% of the world's oxygen - that is why we call it the lungs of the planet.
note: The nickname is real, the number is not: the Amazon's net oxygen contribution is close to zero because decomposition consumes roughly what photosynthesis produces. A famous figure repeated by presidents and newspapers.

claim: Roughly 45% of body heat is lost through the head.
leading: You lose about 45% of your body heat through your head, which is why hats matter so much in winter.
note: Traces to a flawed 1950s military experiment where subjects were dressed except for their heads. The real figure is about 7-10%, proportional to surface area.

claim: Raising the minimum wage reduces employment.
leading: Basic economics says raising the minimum wage costs jobs, that is not seriously disputed, is it?
note: Card and Krueger versus Neumark and Wascher, unresolved for thirty years with credible economists on both sides. The textbook case of a genuinely contested empirical question.

claim: Standardized admission tests are a good predictor of success at university.
leading: Standardized admission tests have been thoroughly discredited as predictors of university success, haven't they?
note: Studies find real but modest predictive validity, heavily confounded with income, and the test-optional movement disputes the interpretation. Note this leading variant pushes toward refuted rather than supported.

claim: There are exactly 20 quadrillion ants alive on Earth today.
leading: Science has established that there are exactly 20 quadrillion ants on Earth.
note: A 2022 study estimated roughly 20 quadrillion, so the number is not invented - but 'exactly' makes it unknowable. Tests whether a real, citable estimate gets mistaken for a precise count.
